title: Synchronizing Probabilities in Model-Driven Lossless Compression
claim: Probabilities near a bin edge switch to an alternative binning via a helper bit, so small mismatches still quantize identically.
layout: 2 stacked rows, left legend boxes, number lines read left-to-right, arrows on points
description: Two stacked horizontal panels show how PMATIC quantizes a probability on the unit interval. On the left, colored text boxes label each case. Case 1 is pink: the probability is not near an edge, the helper bit is 0, and the original binning is used. Case 2 is blue: the probability is near an edge, the helper bit is 1, and the alternative binning is used. On the right, each row has a number line from 0.0 to 1.0 with ticks at 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75. Pink shaded squares mark the bin edges. Green stars mark quantization points. A magenta dot (case 1) and a blue dot (case 2) show the probability, with curved arrows to where each snaps. Dashed bracket markers in the top right show r = 0.125 and δ = 0.01.
caption: Examples of PMATIC helper-bit and quantization logic for two cases, one where the helper bit is $0$ and one where the helper bit is $1$.
abstract: It is well-known in the field of lossless data compression that probabilistic next-symbol prediction can be used to compress sequences of symbols. Deep neural networks are able to capture rich dependencies in data, offering a powerful means of estimating these probabilities and hence an avenue towards more effective compression algorithms. However, both compressor and decompressor must have exactly matching predictions; even small differences from non-determinism (which often happen with learned models due to hardware, software, or computation order) can lead to cascading decoding failures. In this paper, we formalize the problem of prediction mismatch in model-driven compression, and introduce Probability Matching Interval Coding (PMATIC), a model-agnostic algorithm that tolerates bounded prediction mismatch with low overhead. PMATIC works with the predicted probabilities, making it compatible as a drop-in replacement for the arithmetic encoder in model-driven compression tools. We show theoretical correctness and performance bounds for PMATIC, and validate these results on text data. These results confirm that, when paired an advanced prediction model, PMATIC is robust to prediction mismatch while achieving compression rates that out-perform standard modern compression tools.
